title: #53 Ask Students to Put Their Mini-Whiteboards Together
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton recounts a coaching visit where a paired mini-whiteboard discussion fizzled despite a range of answers, because students simply traded one-line answers without real dialogue. His fix was a small physical tweak: ask students to place their mini-whiteboards between them during the paired discussion rather than each holding their own. The next day, with the same class, the change produced a marked shift -- students leaned into the shared space, launched straight into explaining their working instead of sitting through an awkward silence, and used the board's contents as a shared reference point for comparing methods and answers. Barton frames the boards-between-them positioning as a catalyst that converts a stilted answer-swap into genuine discussion, since students can point to specific steps rather than only exchanging final answers. He closes by suggesting the tweak pairs well with a set of follow-up questions he has written about elsewhere for extending paired talk.
points: A tiny physical change -- placing mini-whiteboards between partners rather than each holding their own -- visibly altered students' body language and drew them into shared attention on the work.
Without a shared object to reference, paired discussion collapsed into a bare exchange of final answers rather than actual reasoning.
Even when partners had the same answer, comparing their boards revealed different methods, giving them something substantive to discuss instead of ending the conversation early.
The mini-whiteboard becomes a natural frame of reference that prompts students to notice and explain similarities and differences in approach.
quotes: One student told their partner their answer, their partner then said what they got, and then things kind of fizzled out.
I suggested a tiny tweak: ask the students to put their mini-whiteboards in between them during the paired discussion.
The students’ body positions changed. Instead of sitting upright, they leaned into the space between them to focus on their boards.
There was no awkward silence as there often can be at the start of paired discussions.
But the most important difference was how quickly the dialogue turned from: I think this… I think this… into an actual discussion.
Even when answers were the same (see the second picture), the mini-whiteboards revealed a different approach, which again gave students something to talk about.
